BIOL 345 Principles of Ecology and BIOL 345L Ecology Lab — Fall 2026

Updated 2026-08-20

## Instructor

Dr. Chris Merkord, Associate Professor, Department of Biosciences, Minnesota State University Moorhead

See D2L for email contact information, office hours, and meeting scheduling links.

## Course Description

The structure and function of ecological systems. With lab and field work that will emphasize local species and ecosystems.

Prerequisites: none.

Credits: 4

### Class Meetings

#### Lectures

Mondays and Wednesdays 1:30-2:45 PM in Weld Hall 013.

#### Labs

Thursday 9:00–11:50 AM

Classes meet in Hagen Hall room 410 unless otherwise noted on the class schedule. Field trips depart promptly at the start of class, anyone not there on time will be left.

Field trips travel by university vehicle to the Regional Science Center, located 16 miles east of Moorhead off Hwy 10. The address is 663 164th St S, Glyndon, MN 56547 and directions can be found here: <https://www2.mnstate.edu/science-center/directions.aspx>

### Communicating with the instructor

All email correspondence to course instructors must originate from your university email account, have your full name in the body of the email, and contain the course number “BIOL 345” in the subject line. E-mails not meeting these requirements may not be recognized by the instructor’s email filter and thus may not be answered. The easiest way to meet these requirements is to use the email function in D2L (the envelope icon at the top of the page).

I generally answer messages within 24 hours, Monday through Friday 9 AM-5 PM (except holidays). When other circumstances arise, for example when I am traveling for a conference or travel course, the response time will be longer. Those situations will be announced on D2L ahead of time.

I expect students to check D2L and their university email address once per day.

### Required Texts

- SimUText Ecology, pubished by SimBio (Purchase instructions will be provided in class and on D2L)

### Course Objectives/Student Learning Outcomes

1.  To become familiar with the ecology of Minnesota, including tall grass prairie ecosystems.
2.  To develop skills necessary for understanding, interpreting, and communicating the results of ecological experiments.
3.  To gain an overview of current theories of ecology.

### Outline of Major Content Areas

#### Ecological Concepts

- Physiological ecology (evapotranspiration, water potential, adaptation, acclimation, homeostasis, photosynthesis, metabolism)
- Biogeography (biodiversity, extinction crisis, island biogeography, biomes, speciation, global patterns)
- Ecosystem ecology (energy flows, production, respiration)
- Nutrient cycling (water, nitrogen, carbon, human impacts)
- Decomposition (rates, aerobic vs. anaerobic, litter quality, decomposer organisms)
- Population ecology (growth models, dispersal, metapopulations)
- Biotic interactions (predation, herbivory, competition, mutualism)
- Community dynamics (disturbance, succession, food chains)
- Behavioral ecology (foraging)
- Urban ecology
- Climate change

#### Knowledge and Skills

- Minnesota ecoregions (climate, soil, plant and animal species)
- Field data collection and data entry
- Keeping a field notebook
- Identifying organisms using keys, field guides, and iNaturalist
- Prairie plant identification and various vegetation assessments
- Tree identification and various vegetation assessments
- Fish seining and identification
- Basic data analysis in R and RStudio
- Science communication - oral presentation

### Associated Life Science Teaching Goals

**6.A.2.b** : - design a mathematical model to provide a reasonable fit to a given set of data;

**6.B.4.a** : - describe in words, pictures, and diagrams the range of physical, behavioral, and biochemical adaptations that can occur in response to environmental stresses for a given species;

**6.B.5.b** : - perform measurements and statistical analyses to describe the diversity and number of species in a given ecosystem;

**6.B.5.c** : - describe, using words, pictures, and diagrams, the cycling of a given substance among living and nonliving components of the biosphere;

**6.B.5.d** : - describe, using words, pictures, diagrams, and simple mathematical relationships, the cycling of matter and the flow of energy both within a given system, and between the system and the biosphere;

**6.B.5.e** : - explain, using the relationships between biotic and abiotic components of that system, why the population size and diversity of species is different between two different niches, habitats, ecosystems, or biomes;

**6.B.5.f** : - explain and predict, using population growth dynamics and interspecific and intraspecific interactions, changes in population size of organisms in an ecosystem for a given change in the biotic and abiotic components of the ecosystem;

**6.B.5.g** : - design an experiment to investigate relationships within and among species in a simple ecosystem

## Course Policies

### Instructional Strategies

You will be expected to read each chapter of the SimUText Ecology book/software, answer the interactive questions, and take the quizzes [before coming to class]{.underline} (see course schedule for due dates)

Class time will generally consist of chapter discussions and will involve your peers. Be prepared to participate! You don’t have to know everything (or why would you be taking this class?!) but you are encouraged to:

1.  Ask lots of questions and to bring up issues you are thinking and wondering about.
2.  Listen to the questions and issues brought up by your colleagues.

Labs will involve a combination of hands-on outdoor field-based activities, dry lab activities, and computer lab activities.

### Grades and Assessment

Grades will be assigned using an A, B, C, D, F scale based on the percentage of total points earned, as follows:

- A 90–100 %
- B 80–89.99 %
- C 70–79.99 %
- D 60–69.99 %
- F less than 60 %

Grades for individual quizzes, exams, assignments, etc. will be graded using a minimum grade approach to ensure equitable outcomes for all students. For any assignment, if you earn a grade less than 50%, your grade will be adjusted up to 50%. This applies even if you do not complete an assignment. A 50% is still a failing grade. This approach makes it easier for students to overcome some missing assignments or poor exam scores by grading assignments on a scale more similar to the 4.0 scale used for the course as a whole.

There are four categories of points: exams, comprehension checks, lab activities, and lab project, with percentages assigned as follows:

| Category                           | Points |
|------------------------------------|--------|
| SimUText Assignments               | 28     |
| Class Engagement                   | 10     |
| Unintended Consequences Assignment | 8      |
| Seminars                           | 2      |
| Labs                               | 30     |
| Midterm Exam                       | 7      |
| Lab Practical                      | 7      |
| Final Exam                         | 8      |

#### SimUText Assignments

For most class periods, there will be an assignment to complete before class using the SimBio Active Learning System, a browser-based interactive textbook and quiz platform. All SimUText assignments will be made available at the beginning of the semester or after the midterm, so you may work ahead if you wish. Due dates and times will also be visible within the SimBio Active Learning System.

##### Important Dates and Times

For each SimUText assignment:

- **Sunday at 11:59 PM:** Assignment is due.
- **After Sunday at 11:59 PM:** The assignment may still be completed with a 20% late penalty on answers submitted after that time. Answers submitted before that time do not receive a penalty.
- **Start of class on Monday:** The assignment closes and scores become visible. No additional answers may be submitted after this time except by students with approved extended due dates.
- **End of class on Monday:** Grades become visible.

You may change your answers to any questions until the assignment due date.

##### Scoring

Each assignment is worth a different number of points depending on the number and types of questions it contains.

Feedback questions are interspersed throughout each chapter. You receive credit for a feedback question if you provide an answer, even if your answer is incorrect. Be sure not to leave feedback questions blank, as unanswered feedback questions receive no credit.

Graded questions appear at the end of each section. You receive credit for graded questions only when you answer them correctly.

- Each feedback question is worth **1 point**.
- Each graded question is worth **2 points**.
- On average, approximately **two-thirds of the available points** come from feedback questions and **one-third** from graded questions, but this varies by chapter.

Scores are calculated automatically based on your submitted answers but are not visible until the start of the class in which the assignment will be discussed. Grades become visible at the end of class.

##### Late Work

SimUText assignments are due at **11:59 PM on the Sunday before the class in which the assignment will be discussed**. Because all assignments are available well in advance, students are expected to plan ahead and complete assignments by the posted deadline.

Assignments submitted after the Sunday 11:59 PM deadline but before the start of class receive a **20% late penalty**. At the start of class, the assignment closes and scores become visible. No additional responses may be submitted after that time unless the student has an approved extension.

##### Extensions

Extensions are intended for circumstances that substantially interfere with a student's ability to complete coursework, rather than routine scheduling difficulties.

A qualifying circumstance is a university- or instructor-approved activity, condition, or situation that substantially interferes with a student's ability to complete coursework. When a qualifying circumstance affects a student during the seven calendar days preceding the assignment deadline, the deadline will normally be extended by one calendar day for each day affected.

Students should email the instructor to request an extension as soon as reasonably possible.

Circumstances known well in advance generally do not warrant an extension because SimUText assignments are available well in advance and can be completed early. Students should plan to complete assignments before anticipated conflicts. Similarly, ordinary scheduling pressures—such as having a busy week, multiple exams or assignments, employment obligations, or other foreseeable demands—do not normally qualify for an extension.

Extended or serious circumstances that substantially interfere with coursework for a longer period will be considered individually and handled in accordance with applicable university policies.

Students with an approved extension will receive an adjusted due date. The new due date will also be the date the student's scores are published and the answers become visible. There is no late-submission window for an extended due date.

#### Class Engagement

#### Class Engagement

Many class periods will include interactive activities, discussions, demonstrations, polls, problem-solving exercises, or other opportunities to engage with course material. These activities are an important part of the course, and you are expected to attend class prepared to participate.

Class engagement points will be awarded for participating in designated in-class activities. These points are based primarily on participation and engagement rather than whether every response is correct. Simply being present in class does not necessarily earn engagement points; you must participate in the activity as directed.

Class engagement may take a variety of forms, including:

- responding to questions or polls;
- participating in small-group or class discussions;
- completing in-class exercises or problem-solving activities;
- participating in demonstrations or other interactive activities; and
- providing feedback to your peers on their Unintended Consequences project presentations.

Because these activities depend on what occurs during a particular class period, class engagement points ordinarily cannot be made up outside of class.

To allow for occasional missed classes or activities, the **lowest 10% of your scored class engagement grade items will be dropped** when your final course grade is calculated. This allowance is intended to accommodate occasional circumstances that prevent participation without requiring make-up work.

If a university- or instructor-approved circumstance results in a more substantial disruption that is not adequately addressed by the 10% drop, contact the instructor. Appropriate adjustments will be made so that an approved circumstance does not reduce your course grade.

Class engagement is intended to encourage regular participation in the learning process, not to penalize mistakes or uncertainty. You are encouraged to contribute ideas, ask questions, attempt problems, provide constructive feedback to your peers, and participate in discussions even when you are not certain of the answer.

#### Unintended Consequences Project

Teams of students (n = 3 per team) will develop and give a presentation explaining the interconnectedness of two seemingly unrelated things. Teams will identify and explain the ecological concepts necessary for understanding these connections and classify the system properties relevant to their example. The goal of the project is to demonstrate your ability to apply ecological concepts and systems thinking to connections that may not initially appear obvious.

Each team will choose the specific topic for its project within bounds established by the instructor. This gives teams an opportunity to pursue examples that interest them while ensuring that projects are appropriate for the goals and scope of the assignment. Detailed instructions for selecting a topic, developing the project, and preparing the presentation will be posted separately.

##### Project Components and Grading

The project will be evaluated using a grading rubric posted on D2L. Project points will be awarded for three components:

- **Instructor check-in:** Each team will check in with the instructor in advance of the presentation. At the check-in, the team should be prepared to discuss its topic, preliminary research and analysis, planned approach, and the responsibilities of individual team members. The check-in provides an opportunity to identify problems and receive feedback while there is still time to improve the project.
- **Presentation document:** Each team will submit the document or other presentation materials used to communicate its analysis. The presentation document will be evaluated according to the criteria provided in the grading rubric.
- **In-class presentation:** Each team will present its work to the class. All team members are expected to participate meaningfully in the presentation. The presentation will be evaluated according to the criteria provided in the grading rubric.

Specific requirements, deadlines, point values, and the grading rubric will be provided on D2L.

##### Team and Individual Contributions

Although this is a team project, each student is responsible for making a meaningful contribution to the project as a whole. This includes contributing to the research and analysis, preparation and development of the presentation document, and in-class presentation. Participating only in the final presentation does not constitute a complete contribution to the project.

Team members do not need to contribute identical amounts of work or perform identical tasks. Teams may divide responsibilities according to members' skills, interests, and the needs of the project. However, each member is expected to contribute substantively and reliably to the team's work.

The team scores for the project components will normally serve as the starting point for each student's project grade. However, individual grades may be adjusted when there is evidence that a student's contribution was substantially greater or less than the contributions of other team members.

##### Peer Evaluation and Individual Accountability

Following the presentation, students **may be asked to complete a confidential peer evaluation** describing their own contribution and the contributions of the other members of their team. Peer evaluations may address areas such as:

- contribution to research and analysis;
- contribution to preparation and development of the presentation;
- reliability and collaboration with the team; and
- contribution to the in-class presentation.

Peer evaluations provide information to the instructor; students do not assign grades to their teammates. When peer evaluations are used, the instructor may consider them along with observations during the instructor check-in and presentation and other available evidence when determining whether individual grade adjustments are appropriate.

Students who are concerned that a team member is not contributing should contact the instructor **before the project is due**. The instructor check-in is also an opportunity to identify problems with participation or the division of responsibilities while there is still time to address them.

#### Seminars

You must attend at least two seminars outside of class and submit a reflection for each. Seminars must be at least 30 minutes long and have a substantive connection to ecology.

##### Qualifying Seminars

Both in-person and live virtual seminars qualify. Examples of seminar opportunities include:

- the Bioscience Department's Friday Research Exploration and Education (FREE) seminar series;
- seminars offered by other departments or programs, such as Sustainability;
- seminars at other universities or research institutions; and
- other live presentations with a substantive connection to ecology.

Announcements of upcoming seminar opportunities will be posted as D2L announcements. This list is not exhaustive, and you are encouraged to find other seminars that interest you. If you are unsure whether a seminar will qualify, contact the instructor before attending it for credit.

Prerecorded presentations that you find independently do not qualify. Near the end of the semester, the instructor will provide a list of approved prerecorded seminars for students who have been unable to complete the required number of live seminars. These approved recordings may be used to complete the seminar requirement.

##### Seminar Reflections

For each seminar, you must submit a reflection on D2L identifying the presentation you attended and explaining its connection to ecology. Additional requirements for the reflection are provided in the **Ecology Seminar Instructions** on D2L.

All seminar reflections must be submitted by the seminar assignment deadline posted on D2L near the end of the semester. You do not need to wait until the deadline to submit them.

##### Required Credit and Extra Credit

The first **two qualifying seminars** and their associated reflections are required. You may complete up to two additional seminar assignments for extra credit:

- **Seminars 1–2:** required

- **Seminar 3:** 1 point of extra credit

- **Seminar 4:** 1 additional point of extra credit

Thus, you may receive credit for a maximum of four seminar assignments and earn up to **2 points of extra credit**.

#### Lab Assignments

Labs are an important part of this course and will involve field observations, data collection, group activities, and other applications of ecological concepts and methods. Requirements will vary among labs, and the handout for each lab will identify the activities to complete, what should be recorded in your field notebook, and any additional work that must be submitted. Lab grades will reflect both your participation in the lab and the work you produce.

##### Lab Engagement

Part of each lab score will be based on your **engagement during the lab period**. Engagement will be assessed during lab and includes actively participating in assigned activities, working productively with your group when applicable, following instructions and appropriate procedures, and contributing to the collection, interpretation, or discussion of data and observations.

Simply being present for lab does not necessarily earn full engagement credit. You are expected to participate actively in the work of the lab.

##### Field Notebook

Careful observation and documentation are fundamental skills in field ecology. Your field notebook provides a record of what you did, observed, and measured in the field and allows you to return to those observations later for analysis and interpretation.

You should make a field notebook entry for each field lab. **The handout for each lab will specify what should be recorded in your field notebook for that activity.** Because field activities differ, the specific information required will vary from one lab to another.

Each field notebook entry should include:

- the **date and time** of the field activity;

- the **location** of the activity;

- the **names of your team members**;

- what you did;

- observations made during the field activity;

- measurements and raw data, when appropriate;

- relevant sketches, diagrams, or other visual records, when appropriate; and

- enough context and explanation that you or another reader could understand the record later.

Some labs may use **separate data sheets** for recording particular measurements or datasets rather than requiring all data to be copied into the field notebook. The lab handout will specify when separate data sheets should be used and what information should be recorded in the field notebook.

Your primary observations, measurements, data, and other records should be entered in your field notebook **during the lab while the work is being conducted**. You may add to your entry afterward—for example, by adding calculations, interpretations, identifications, conclusions, or connections to course concepts—but these additions should supplement rather than replace the record you made in the field.

At the end of each field lab, a Learning Assistant or the instructor will briefly check your notebook entry for completion. You will receive a completion score and may receive brief feedback about aspects of your field notes that should be improved in subsequent entries. These checks are intended to help you develop good field-note practices over the course of the semester.

Your complete field notebook will be collected and graded **once, after the final field lab**. This grade will consider the completeness, organization, and quality of your field notebook entries across the field portion of the course.

##### Additional Lab Assignments

Some labs will require an additional product, such as a worksheet, data analysis, report, or other written assignment. Instructions and submission requirements will be provided in the individual lab handout. Not every lab will require an additional assignment.

##### Lab Grades

Points associated with lab work may therefore come from several sources:

- **Lab engagement:** active participation during the lab;

- **Field notebook completion:** a brief check at the end of each field lab;

- **Field notebook grade:** an evaluation of the complete notebook after the final field lab; and

- **Additional lab assignments:** worksheets, analyses, write-ups, reports, or other assigned products when required.

The requirements for each lab will be specified in its lab handout.

#### Midterm Exam

This exam will cover material from both lecture and laboratory.

It may include objective questions in a variety of formats (multiple choice, figure interpretations, numeric calculations, short answer, essay, sketches, and concept maps). There will be an emphasis on open-ended questions and problem solving opportunities. Long answer questions will be handed out in person the period before the exam so that you may think about how to answer them during the exam.

*In order to be successful, you must be able to demonstrate comprehension by explaining course concepts in your own words and applying your knowledge to new situations.*

#### Lab Practical. Details TBD.

#### Final Exam

This will be like the Midterm Exam. It will not be comprehensive, i.e. it will only cover material from the second half of the course.
